input: It is worth noting that gravity settling represents a well-established and widely utilised unit operation for the separation of solid particles from liquid streams, and in the present case it is applied to the removal of calcium carbonate from a process stream. In a gravity settler, the incoming stream is distributed across the plan area of the vessel, the solid particles gradually settle downwards under the influence of gravity towards the base, and a clarified liquid stream is withdrawn over a weir at the top of the unit. The sizing of such a unit is fundamentally governed by the overflow rate, which can be defined as the volumetric throughput divided by the plan area of the settler. At a throughput of 67 m3 h-1 and a design overflow rate of 1.51 m h-1, the required plan area works out to 44 m2. The underlying principle here is that a particle will be successfully removed if its settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate, whereas a particle that settles more slowly will inevitably be carried out with the clarified liquid, which means that the overflow rate effectively acts as the dividing line between the particles that are captured and those that are not. It should nevertheless be emphasised that the design overflow rate adopted here is derived from a vendor rule for this particular solid, and, crucially, no settling test has actually been carried out on the real slurry, so the vendor value may or may not be representative of the actual material, whose particle size distribution and solids concentration could differ in various respects. This introduces a degree of uncertainty into the stated area, and the consequences of any error are not necessarily symmetric, since an undersized unit would pass solids onwards to downstream equipment while an oversized unit would mainly attract additional cost. Overall, the stated sizing should therefore be viewed as a preliminary, vendor-based estimate, and a settling test on a representative sample of the actual slurry would clearly be a valuable next step in order to place the design on a firmer footing going forward.
target: A gravity settler removes calcium carbonate from a process stream. Liquid enters the vessel, solids settle under gravity to the base, and clarified liquid leaves over a weir at the top. Sizing is set by the overflow rate, defined as the volumetric throughput divided by the plan area of the settler. A particle is removed when its settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate; a particle that settles more slowly leaves with the clarified liquid, and the overflow rate is the cut between the two outcomes. At a throughput of 67 m3 h-1 and a design overflow rate of 1.51 m h-1, the plan area is 44 m2. The design rate comes from a vendor rule for calcium carbonate. No settling test has been run on the actual slurry, and the vendor material may differ from the stream treated here in particle size distribution and solids concentration. The stated area therefore carries an unquantified error in either direction. The consequences are not symmetric. An undersized settler passes solids to the downstream equipment, where carryover appears as fouling or off-specification product; an oversized settler costs vessel volume and plot space but leaves the separation intact. A settling test on a representative sample of the actual slurry would replace the vendor rule with a measured rate for this solid in this liquid, and would also show how the rate varies with feed concentration. Any later change in throughput at a fixed area moves the operating overflow rate in direct proportion, and a rate pushed above the settling velocity of a larger share of the solids degrades the separation in proportion. Until the test is run, the stated area supports a preliminary vessel size and an order for the test itself; it is not a measured performance figure, and the design should be revisited once a measured settling rate for the actual slurry is available.
